text: This lesson is about semaphores and node usage — a core piece of ServiceNow platform architecture that explains a lot of real-world slowness that isn't actually about any one request being slow to process at all.

A production instance typically runs across multiple application nodes for capacity and resilience, not just one machine handling everything alone. More nodes means more total capacity, but every node still needs its own way to stop one category of work from monopolizing its resources and starving everything else trying to run on it at the same time.

That's exactly what a semaphore does. It's a concurrency-control mechanism: a hard limit on how many requests of a certain type can run simultaneously, per node. Background and scheduled work is one major category. Specific transaction types are others. Each category gets its own pool of execution slots, rather than every request being lumped into one giant, undifferentiated queue.

This separation protects the whole node. Without it, one runaway category — say, background jobs — could consume every available thread on that node, taking interactive performance down with it as collateral damage. Bounded, separate pools guarantee that even a fully saturated background queue still leaves interactive transactions their own reserved slots to run in.

Here's the critical diagnostic point of this whole lesson. When every slot in a semaphore's pool is busy — semaphore exhaustion — new requests of that same type have to queue and wait their turn. To the end user, that wait looks exactly like ordinary slowness. But the real cause isn't the request being inherently slow — it's sitting in line, waiting for a spot in an already-full pool.

Treating that queue delay as if it were ordinary request slowness leads straight to the wrong fix — optimizing a script that was never actually running slowly in the first place. The real fix targets the contention itself. Next up, we'll look at one of the most common real-world causes of exactly this kind of contention: Scheduled Jobs.
